A user tried LlamaParse and was impressed by the result on a document with a complex layout. They said none of the open-source parsers gave results that were even close.

A user was confused by the published benchmarks. The baseline was PyPDF + naive RAG, while LlamaParse was evaluated with a different 'recursive retrieval' pipeline. When they re-ran the baseline code themselves, they got a faithfulness score of 0.980 versus the reported 0.667. That was higher than the score reported for the LlamaParse-based solution.

Criticism in the LlamaParse thread: making something look like an open source library when it is actually just a wrapper around a paid hosted service is described as endemic in Python and especially the LLM space.
"LlamaParse solves exactly the problem I've encountered over and over with RAG. Getting structured info from unstructured data is a pain."
A commenter objected that LlamaIndex built community attention as open source and then launched a proprietary parsing service. They compared it to LangChain and other "fake open source" projects.

A user found the interface a bit confusing. LlamaParse can extract numbers in tables, but the output didn't appear to be in tabular format, so the numbers seemed accessible only through question-answering.

A user was unimpressed by their initial experience. Email sign-up endlessly redirected (click the email link, get asked to sign up again), so they had to use Google sign-in. They also questioned the need for it given PDFBox, iText, Unstructured, PyPDF, PDF.js, PdfMiner and hyperscaler extraction services.

A user compared LlamaParse to AWS Textract, which already parses and queries tables and forms. They conceded that integration into a LlamaIndex RAG workflow may be convenient, but asked why reinvent the wheel.
